questions.question: Define the photoelectric effect, threshold frequency and work function, state the relationship between the last two, and explain why the effect is regarded as evidence for the particle nature of light, naming the three observations the wave model cannot explain.
questions.expected_answer: The photoelectric effect is the process whereby electrons are ejected from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency shines on it. The threshold frequency f₀ is the minimum light frequency that will eject electrons from a particular metal; the work function W₀ is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from that metal's surface; they are linked by W₀ = hf₀. Evidence for particle nature: the wave model predicts that energy accumulates continuously, so any frequency should work at sufficient brightness, faint light should cause a delay, and brightness should control electron energy. Observation contradicts all three: (1) emission is instantaneous even in very faint light; (2) there is a sharp frequency threshold below which no emission occurs regardless of intensity; (3) the maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not on brightness. Only energy arriving in indivisible packets — photons of energy E = hf, one photon absorbed by one electron — explains all three, so light must have a particle nature (complementing the wave nature shown by interference and diffraction).

questions.question: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a sodium surface with work function 3,65 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the frequency of the light, the photon energy, the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons and sodium's threshold frequency, and explain why the ejected electrons do not all have the same kinetic energy.
questions.expected_answer: Frequency: f = c/λ = (3 × 10⁸)/(4,0 × 10⁻⁷) = 7,5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Photon energy: E = hf = (6,63 × 10⁻³⁴)(7,5 × 10¹⁴) = 4,97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Since 4,97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J > W₀, emission occurs. Maximum kinetic energy: E k max = E − W₀ = (4,97 − 3,65) × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1,32 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency: f₀ = W₀/h = (3,65 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6,63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 5,51 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The spread of kinetic energies arises because the equation books only the best case: electrons ejected from the very surface pay only the work function, while electrons escaping from deeper in the metal lose additional energy on the way out and therefore emerge with less than the maximum kinetic energy.

questions.question: Distinguish the effects of increasing the intensity and increasing the frequency of light on photoelectric emission (above and below the threshold). Then explain how atomic emission and absorption spectra arise, why they consist of discrete lines, and how they let astronomers identify elements in stars.
questions.expected_answer: Intensity: more photons per second, each of unchanged energy hf. Above threshold this ejects more electrons per second (larger photocurrent) with unchanged maximum kinetic energy; below threshold it achieves nothing, since no electron can combine two photons' energies. Frequency: more energy per photon. Above threshold each electron leaves with greater maximum kinetic energy, but the number per second is unchanged unless the photon rate changes. Spectra: an atom's electrons occupy only fixed energy levels. When an electron drops from level E₂ to E₁ the atom emits one photon with E = hf = E₂ − E₁, so a hot gas emits only its own set of frequencies — bright, sharp lines on black (emission spectrum). White light through the same cool gas has exactly those frequencies absorbed as electrons jump upward, leaving dark lines on a continuous rainbow (absorption spectrum) at identical positions. Lines are discrete because energy levels are quantised — no in-between energies exist. Since each element has a unique level ladder, its line pattern is a fingerprint: the dark lines in a star's spectrum identify the elements in its atmosphere (helium was found in sunlight this way), and a uniformly shifted pattern reveals the star's motion.
